fear.e: From Middle English feer, fere, fer (“fear”), from Old English fǣr, ġefǣr (“calamity, sudden danger, peril, sudden attack, terrible sight”), from Proto-Germanic *fērō, *fērą (“danger”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through, carry forth, try”).
fear.g: A strong, unpleasant emotion or feeling caused by actual or perceived danger or threat.

fear.e: From Middle English fere, feore, from Old English fēre (“able to go, fit for service”), from Proto-Germanic *fēriz (“passable”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to put across, ferry”).

feared.e: From Middle English ferd, feerd, fered, equivalent to fear + -ed.

fearful.e: From Middle English ferful, fervol, equivalent to fear + -ful.

feast.e: From Middle English feeste, feste, borrowed from Old French feste, from Late Latin festa, from the plural of Latin festum (“holiday, festival, feast”), from Proto-Italic *fēs-tos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”); see also Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god, goddess”).
feast.g: A holiday, festival, especially a religious one

feast.e: From Middle English feesten, festen, from Old French fester, from Medieval Latin festāre, from the noun.
feast.g: To partake in a feast, or large meal.

feather.e: From Middle English fethere, from Old English feþer, from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”). The sense correlated with splines and keys (noun sense 4) probably reflects analogy with the fletching sense (noun sense 3).
feather.g: A branching, hair-like structure that grows on the bodies of birds, used for flight, swimming, protection and display.

fed.g: A federal government officer or official.
A federation in which powerlifters organize to compete.

fee.e: From Middle English fee, fe, feh, feoh, from Old English feoh (“cattle, property, wealth, money, payment, tribute, fee”) with contamination from Old French fieu, fief (from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (see feud), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”); whence fief), both from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle, sheep, livestock, owndom”).
fee.g: An amount charged in return for permission to do something

feeble.e: From Middle English feble, from Anglo-Norman feble (“weak, feeble”) (compare French faible), from Latin flēbilis (“tearful, mournful, lamentable”) by dissimilation, from fleō (“to weep, cry”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-.

feebleness.e: From Middle English feblenesse; equivalent to feeble + -ness.
feebleness.g: The quality or state of being feeble; debility; infirmity.

feed.e: From Middle English feden, from Old English fēdan (“to feed”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to guard, graze, feed”).
feed.g: To give (someone or something) food to eat.

feed.e: From Middle English fede, fed, from the verb (see above). Alternatively, perhaps from Old Norse fœða (“nourishment, food”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), whence also Old English fēdan (“to feed”).
feed.g: Food given to (especially herbivorous) non-human animals.

feeding.g: The act or process of giving food.

feel.e: From Middle English felen, from Old English fēlan, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan.
feel.g: To use or experience the sense of touch.

feeling.e: From Middle English felynge, equivalent to feel + -ing.

feign.e: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”).
feign.g: To make a false show or pretence of; to counterfeit or simulate.

feignedly.g: In a way that is feigned.

fell.e: From Middle English fellen, from Old English fellan, fiellan (“to cause to fall, strike down, fell, cut down, throw down, defeat, destroy, kill, tumble, cause to stumble”), from Proto-West Germanic *fallijan, from Proto-Germanic *fallijaną (“to fell, to cause to fall”), causative of Proto-Germanic *fallaną (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂peh₃lH-.
fell.g: To make something fall, especially a tree.

fell.e: From Middle English fell, fel, vel, from Old English fel, fell (“hide, skin, pelt”), from Proto-West Germanic *fell, from Proto-Germanic *fellą, from Proto-Indo-European *pél-no- (“skin, animal hide”).

feller.e: From Middle English fellere, feller; equivalent to fell + -er.
feller.g: A person who fells trees; a lumberjack

feller.e: Variant of fellow that reflects the reduction of the last vowel to a schwa and its conflation with the endings -er/-ar.

felloe.e: From Middle English felwe, from Old English felg (“harrow, felloe”).
felloe.g: The rim of a wooden wheel, supported by the spokes.

fellow.e: From Middle English felawe, felowe (“companion, good friend”) from Old English fēolaga, from Old Norse félagi, derived from félag (“joint venture; partnership”, literally “a laying together of property”), from fé (“livestock, property; money”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“livestock; wealth”)) + lag (“something laid down; right position.
From Middle English felauen, felow (“to join (someone) in companionship, friendship, partnership, etc.”), from felowe, felau, felawe (noun): see etymology 1.
fellow.g: To address (someone) as "fellow", especially in an insulting manner (see noun sense 10.6).

fellowship.e: From Middle English felowschipe, felawshipe, felaȝschyp, equivalent to fellow + -ship; or perhaps adapted from Old Norse félagskapr, félagsskapr (“fellowship”).
fellowship.g: A company of people that share the same interest or aim.

felt.e: From Old English fēled, corresponding to feel + -ed.
felt.g: That has been experienced or perceived.

female.e: From Middle English female, an alteration of Middle English femele, from Old French femele, femelle (“female”), from Medieval Latin fēmella (“a female”), from Latin fēmella (“a girl, a young female, a young woman”), diminutive of fēmina (“a woman”).
female.g: One of the female (feminine) sex or gender.

fen.e: From Middle English fen, fenne, from Old English fenn (“fen; marsh; mud; dirt”), Proto-West Germanic *fani, from Proto-Germanic *fanją, from Proto-Indo-European *pen- (“bog, mire”).
fen.g: A type of wetland fed by ground water and runoff, containing peat below the waterline, characteristically alkaline.

fen.e: From Middle English *vene, Kentish variant of *fine, from Old English fyne (“moisture, mold, mildew”), from Proto-Germanic *funiz, *fun- (“moisture, mold”); compare vinew.
fen.g: A kind of mildew that grows on hops.

fence.e: From Middle English fence, fens, short for defence, defens (“the act of defending”), from Old French defens, defense (see defence). The sense "enclosure" arises in the mid 15th century. The generalized sense "to defend, screen, protect" arises ca. 1500. The sense "to fight with swords (rapiers)" is from the 1590s (Shakespeare).
fence.g: A thin artificial barrier that separates two pieces of land or forms a perimeter enclosing the lands of a house, building, etc.

ferment.e: From Middle English ferment, from Middle French ferment, from Latin fermentāre (“to leaven, ferment”), from fermentum (“substance causing fermentation”), possibly from contraction of *fervimentum, from fervēre.
ferment.g: To react, using fermentation; especially to produce alcohol by aging or by allowing yeast to act on sugars; to brew.

ferret.e: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).
ferret.g: An often domesticated mammal (Mustela putorius furo) rather like a weasel, descended from the European polecat and often trained to hunt bur
A tape of silk, cotton, or ribbon, used to tie documents, clothing, etc. or along the edge of fabric.

ferry.e: This verb is the causative of Proto-Germanic *faraną (“to go, travel”), whence English fare; ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per-. False cognate of Latin ferō.

fertile.e: From Middle English, from Middle French fertile, from Old French fertile, from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, carry”).
fertile.g: Of land, etc.: capable of growing abundant crops; productive.

fertilize.e: From French fertiliser; equivalent to fertile + -ize.
fertilize.g: To make (the soil) more fertile by adding nutrients to it.

fervent.e: From Middle English fervent, from Old French fervent (modern French fervent), from Latin ferventem, the accusative masculine or feminine singular form of fervēns (“burning, fiery; hot; zealous; etc.”), the present active participle of ferveō (“to burn; to be hot; (figurative) to be agitated, fired up, or inflamed.
fervent.g: Very hot; burning, scorching; also, glowing with heat.

fervently.e: From Middle English fervently; equivalent to fervent + -ly.

fervor.e: From Middle English fervour, from Old French, from Latin fervor (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from fervere (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -or (“abstract noun suffix”).
fervor.g: An intense, heated emotion; passion, ardor.

festal.e: From Middle French festal, from Latin festum (“feast”).
festal.g: festive, relating to a festival or feast

fester.e: From Middle English festre, festur, borrowed from Old French festre (cognate with Italian fistola, Occitan fistola, Spanish fístula), from Latin fistula.

festival.e: From Middle English festival (adjective), from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). By surface analysis, festive + -al.
festival.g: Pertaining to a feast or feast day; festive. (Now only as the noun used attributively.)

festive.e: From French festif, from Latin festivus (“pertaining to a feast, gay, lively, joyous”). Equivalent to feast + -ive.
festive.g: Having the atmosphere, decoration, or attitude of a festival, holiday, or celebration.

fetch.e: The English word is cognate with Dutch vatten (“to apprehend, catch; to grasp; to understand”), German fassen (“to catch, grasp.
fetch.g: To retrieve; to bear towards; to go and get.

fetch.e: Uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: From fetch-life (“(obsolete, rare) a deity, spirit, etc., who guides the soul of a dead person to the afterlife; a psychopomp”). From the supposed Old English *fæcce (“evil spirit formerly thought to sit on the chest of a sleeping person; a mare”). From Old Irish fáith (“seer, soothsayer”).
fetch.g: The apparition of a living person; a person's double, the sight of which is supposedly a sign that they are fated to die soon, a doppelgange

fetter.e: From Middle English feter, from Old English feter, Proto-West Germanic *fetur, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”).
fetter.g: A chain or similar object used to bind a person or animal, often by its legs.

fever.e: From Middle English fever, fevere, from Old English fefer, fefor (“fever”) and Old French fievre (“fever”), from Latin febris (“a fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”).
fever.g: A higher than normal body temperature of a person (or, generally, a mammal), usually caused by disease.

few.e: From Middle English fewe, from Old English fēaw (“few”), from Proto-West Germanic *fau, from Proto-Germanic *fawaz (“few”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).
few.g: An indefinite, but usually small, number of.

foot.e: From Middle English fot, fote, foot, from Old English fōt, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. The plural feet is the result of i-umlaut in Proto-West Germanic *fōti, see more at Old English fōt.
foot.g: A biological structure found in many animals that is used for locomotion and that is frequently a separate organ at the terminal part of the
